nodes.title: HashiCorp Vault tokens: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Tokens are the core authentication mechanism in Vault — every authenticated client uses a token to make API calls. Vault token types, TTLs, and policies determine what a client can do.

flashcards.front: Root token — when and why to use it?
flashcards.back: Generated during 'vault operator init'; has unlimited access. Should be revoked immediately after bootstrapping policies — never used for day-to-day operations.
Service token: stored in Vault, supports renewal, can create child tokens. Batch token: lightweight, encrypted, not stored — cheaper for high-throughput use cases but cannot be renewed or looked up.
TTL: how long until the token expires unless renewed. Max TTL: the absolute ceiling a token's lifetime can be extended to — renewal cannot push past it.
Creates a token without a parent; revocation of the creator's token does not cascade to this token. Useful for long-lived service accounts.

questions.q: You are initializing a new Kubernetes control plane with kubeadm. You want the API server to advertise the IP address 10.0.1.100 to worker nodes. Which kubeadm init flag should you use?
choices: --apiserver-advertise-address=10.0.1.100
--control-plane-endpoint=10.0.1.100
--apiserver-bind-address=10.0.1.100
questions.explanation: --apiserver-advertise-address tells kubeadm which IP address the API server should publish to members of the cluster — that is the value worker nodes will use to talk to it. --control-plane-endpoint is the stable DNS/VIP used in HA setups behind a load balancer, not the per-node advertised IP. --node-ip is a kubelet flag (consumed by /var/lib/kubelet/kubeadm-flags.env), not a kubeadm init flag. --apiserver-bind-address is also not a kubeadm init flag — kubeadm uses --apiserver-advertise-address to populate the manifest's bind/advertise behaviour.

questions.q: A worker node needs to join an existing cluster but the bootstrap token has expired. Which kubeadm command creates a new join token registered with the cluster?
choices: kubeadm init --regenerate-token
kubeadm token create --print-join-command
kubeadm join --create-token
kubeadm token generate
questions.explanation: `kubeadm token create --print-join-command` creates a new bootstrap token, registers it with the cluster, and prints the full `kubeadm join` line including the API server endpoint, token, and CA-cert hash. `kubeadm token generate` only prints a random token string — it does not register it. `kubeadm init --regenerate-token` is not a real subcommand (init bootstraps a new cluster). `kubeadm join --create-token` is also invented — join consumes a token, it does not mint one.

questions.q: A cluster admin is upgrading a kubeadm-managed cluster from Kubernetes v1.29 to v1.30. To respect the version-skew policy and minimise disruption, which overall order is correct?
choices: Upgrade all workers (kubelet + kube-proxy) first, then upgrade every control plane node in parallel using kubeadm upgrade apply
Upgrade etcd only and let the rest of the cluster follow once etcd is on the new minor version — kubeadm propagates the rest automatically
First control plane: kubeadm + `kubeadm upgrade apply` → kubelet/kubectl; then the other control plane nodes; then drain and upgrade each worker
Reinstall every node from scratch on the new version because kubeadm explicitly does not support in-place skew upgrades
questions.explanation: The supported order is: (1) on the first control plane, upgrade the kubeadm binary; (2) run `kubeadm upgrade apply v1.30.x` to update the static-pod manifests; (3) upgrade kubelet and kubectl on that node; (4) repeat the same kubelet/kubectl/kubeadm sequence on the other control plane nodes; (5) drain and upgrade each worker. Workers must never run ahead of the control plane — an older control plane cannot manage a newer kubelet. Upgrading etcd alone leaves apiserver/scheduler/controller-manager behind. kubeadm explicitly supports in-place upgrades, so reinstall from scratch is unnecessary.

questions.q: When bootstrapping a cluster with kubeadm, which flag specifies the pod network CIDR that the CNI plugin should use?
choices: --network-plugin-cidr
--pod-network-cidr
--service-cidr
--cluster-cidr
questions.explanation: --pod-network-cidr passes the pod IP range into the cluster configuration so the CNI plugin (Calico, Flannel, Cilium, …) can carve subnets from it. --service-cidr is a separate flag that configures the range for Service ClusterIPs. --cluster-cidr is an internal kube-controller-manager flag (set indirectly via kubeadm), not a kubeadm init flag. --network-plugin-cidr does not exist.

questions.q: You want to add a second control plane node for high availability. After running `kubeadm init phase upload-certs --upload-certs` on the primary control plane, what command format should you use on the new control plane node?
choices: kubeadm join <endpoint>:<port> --token <token> --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<hash> --control-plane --certificate-key <key>
kubeadm join --control-plane --copy-certs-from=<primary-node-ip> --token <token> --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<hash>
kubeadm init --join --control-plane-endpoint=<endpoint> --certificate-key <key> --token <token>
kubeadm join <endpoint>:<port> --token <token> --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<hash> --node-name <new-cp>
questions.explanation: Joining as a control plane needs both --control-plane (so kubeadm promotes the node and starts control-plane static pods) and --certificate-key (so kubeadm can decrypt the PKI material uploaded earlier with `upload-certs`). The plain join command — same flags minus --control-plane and --certificate-key — joins a worker only. There is no --copy-certs-from option in kubeadm; the cert material moves via the uploaded encrypted Secret. `kubeadm init --join` is not a real form (init bootstraps a new cluster, join attaches a node to an existing one).

questions.q: You need to view the current kubeadm cluster configuration stored inside the cluster. In which ConfigMap and namespace is this kept?
choices: ConfigMap 'kubeadm-config' in namespace 'kube-system'
ConfigMap 'kube-config' in namespace 'kube-public'
ConfigMap 'cluster-info' in namespace 'default'
ConfigMap 'cluster-config' in namespace 'kube-node-lease'
questions.explanation: kubeadm persists the ClusterConfiguration (and component-specific configs) in the ConfigMap `kubeadm-config` in the `kube-system` namespace; inspect it with `kubectl get cm kubeadm-config -n kube-system -o yaml`. The `cluster-info` ConfigMap in `kube-public` only holds the discovery endpoint and CA bundle used during node bootstrap, not the full kubeadm configuration. `kube-config` and `cluster-config` are not standard ConfigMaps in any kubeadm-managed cluster.

nodes.title: Where does the cluster store its state?

choices: etcd
kube-proxy
CoreDNS
kubelet

nodes.explanation: etcd is the consistent, distributed key-value store that holds all cluster state. Only the kube-apiserver talks to it directly — every other component reads and writes state through the API server.

nodes.title: Role-based access control: Key Ideas
nodes.content: RBAC assigns permissions to roles, then users to roles — a layer of indirection that scales. Azure's RBAC, AWS's IAM, Kubernetes RBAC, and GCP's IAM all share the same mental model. Mastering one transfers directly to the others.

flashcards.front: Why use roles instead of granting permissions to users directly?
flashcards.back: Roles separate WHO from WHAT. Add a person to a role, they inherit the permissions. Remove them, they lose access instantly. Auditing: 'who can read prod?' becomes 'who's in the prod-readers role?' instead of scanning thousands of user-level policies. Onboarding/offboarding becomes role membership changes, not 500 permission grants.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between a built-in role and a custom role?
flashcards.back: Built-in: cloud-provided, covers common patterns (Owner, Contributor, Reader, Storage Admin). Can't be modified. Custom: you define the exact actions allowed — pick when built-ins are too broad or too narrow. Cost of custom roles: maintenance — every new service adds actions you may need to add.

flashcards.front: Scope — why is it as important as the role?
flashcards.back: Same role at different scopes = wildly different power. 'Contributor' at the subscription scope = god mode on the whole subscription. 'Contributor' on one resource group = limited to that group's resources. Always scope at the smallest unit that's practical — never grant subscription-level if resource-group-level works.

flashcards.front: RBAC vs ABAC — when do you need attributes?
flashcards.back: RBAC: permissions tied to fixed roles. Works great until you need rules like 'engineers can read their own team's resources but not others'. ABAC (attribute-based) evaluates request attributes (user.team, resource.team) at runtime. Most clouds support both — start with RBAC, add ABAC tags when the role explosion becomes painful.

questions.q: You need to grant a ServiceAccount named 'deploy-bot' in the 'ci' namespace read-only access to Deployments across all namespaces. What combination of resources should you create?
choices: A Role with get/list/watch on deployments in every namespace, and a ClusterRoleBinding
A Role and RoleBinding in the 'ci' namespace
A ClusterRole with get/list/watch on deployments, and a RoleBinding in the 'ci' namespace
A ClusterRole with get/list/watch on deployments, and a ClusterRoleBinding referencing the ServiceAccount
questions.explanation: Cluster-wide access requires both halves to be cluster-scoped: a ClusterRole carrying the permissions, and a ClusterRoleBinding that binds the ServiceAccount across all namespaces. A RoleBinding that references a ClusterRole only grants those permissions inside the binding's own namespace. A Role cannot be cluster-scoped at all — even paired with a ClusterRoleBinding it has no effect, because ClusterRoleBindings only accept ClusterRole references. A namespaced Role/RoleBinding pair would limit access to the 'ci' namespace.

questions.q: A developer reports that `kubectl get pods` returns `Error from server (Forbidden)`. Their kubeconfig context points to the right cluster and `kubectl config view` looks clean. What is the most likely root cause?
choices: The kubelet on the developer's laptop is not running
The user or ServiceAccount has no Role/ClusterRole binding granting `get` on `pods`
The developer needs to run `kubectl auth login` to refresh their tokens
The kube-apiserver TLS certificate has expired on the control plane
questions.explanation: A 403 Forbidden response means the request was authenticated and reached the API server, but the RBAC authoriser denied it — the caller has no Role or ClusterRole binding that allows `get` on `pods`. An expired API server certificate would surface earlier as a TLS handshake error, not Forbidden. `kubectl auth login` is not a real subcommand (the kubectl plugin model uses credential plugins or `kubectl oidc-login`). The kubelet runs on cluster nodes, not on client laptops, so its state is irrelevant.

questions.q: You need to verify what actions the ServiceAccount 'reporter' in namespace 'monitoring' can perform. Which kubectl command checks whether it can list pods in that namespace?
choices: kubectl auth can-i list pods --as=system:serviceaccount:monitoring:reporter -n monitoring
kubectl describe serviceaccount reporter -n monitoring
kubectl auth check --user=reporter --verb=list --resource=pods -n monitoring
kubectl get rolebindings -n monitoring | grep reporter
questions.explanation: `kubectl auth can-i` with --as impersonates the named subject and asks the API server's authoriser for a yes/no answer, so it tests the effective permission across Roles AND ClusterRoles. A ServiceAccount is impersonated using the canonical form `system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<name>`. `kubectl describe serviceaccount` shows metadata and mounted tokens but no permission information. `kubectl get rolebindings | grep` only inspects one namespace's RoleBindings and misses ClusterRoleBindings entirely. `kubectl auth check` is not a real subcommand.

questions.q: You need to quickly test whether a newly created ClusterRole `deployment-viewer` provides the correct permissions. A user `alice` should be able to `get` and `list` Deployments cluster-wide. Which sequence of commands validates this?
choices: kubectl get clusterrole deployment-viewer -o yaml && kubectl get clusterrolebinding | grep alice
kubectl describe clusterrolebinding alice-binding
kubectl auth reconcile --as=alice -f role.yaml
kubectl auth can-i get deployments --as=alice && kubectl auth can-i list deployments --as=alice
questions.explanation: `kubectl auth can-i` with `--as` asks the API server's authoriser to evaluate the entire RBAC chain (ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding) for the impersonated user. Running it for both verbs verifies the actual effective permission, which is the only thing that matters. Reading the ClusterRole YAML and grepping ClusterRoleBindings tells you what was authored but not whether the binding actually applies. Describing the binding shows references but doesn't simulate the access decision. `kubectl auth reconcile` applies RBAC manifests; it is not a permission-check command.

correct.useCase: A plugin spec that wires up pod networking; Calico, Cilium, and Flannel are implementations.

distractors.useCase: Bootstraps a new worker node and joins it to the cluster.
Routes external HTTP traffic to Services.
Resolves service names to cluster IPs.

nodes.title: Networking fundamentals: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Networking moves packets between machines using layered protocols (the OSI / TCP-IP stack). Most exam questions test routing decisions, subnetting math, the difference between L2 and L3, and how DNS / DHCP make the whole thing usable for humans.

flashcards.front: What's the difference between Layer 2 and Layer 3?
flashcards.back: L2 (data link) uses MAC addresses to deliver frames inside a single broadcast domain (a switch). L3 (network) uses IP addresses to route packets between networks (a router). Switches do L2; routers do L3.

flashcards.front: How does a subnet mask work?
flashcards.back: The mask splits an IP into a network portion (the high bits, set to 1) and a host portion (the low bits, set to 0). `/24` means the first 24 bits are network = up to 256 hosts (254 usable). `/30` is 4 IPs = 2 hosts — typical for a point-to-point link.

Domain Name System translates human-readable names (`example.com`) into IP addresses. A recursive resolver asks the root, the TLD server (`.com`), and finally the authoritative server for the domain. TTL controls how long answers are cached.

flashcards.front: TCP vs UDP — when do you pick each?
flashcards.back: TCP is reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled — use it when every byte matters (HTTP, SSH, SMTP). UDP is lightweight, no handshake, no retransmit — use it for streaming, gaming, DNS queries, anywhere latency beats reliability.

questions.q: You need a ClusterIP Service for an application and want to assign a specific cluster IP (e.g. 10.96.100.50) inside the service CIDR. Which Service spec field allows this?
choices: spec.clusterIP: '10.96.100.50'
spec.internalIP: '10.96.100.50'
spec.loadBalancerIP: '10.96.100.50'
spec.externalIPs: ['10.96.100.50']
questions.explanation: `spec.clusterIP` accepts an explicit address provided it is inside the configured service CIDR and not already taken — otherwise the API server rejects the create. `spec.loadBalancerIP` only applies to Service type LoadBalancer (and is deprecated on most clouds in favour of provider-specific annotations). `spec.externalIPs` is a list of host IPs that route traffic into the cluster externally, not the cluster-internal VIP. `spec.internalIP` is not a real Service field.

questions.q: A NodePort Service is created for a web application. A developer cannot reach the app at <NodeIP>:30080 from outside the cluster. The pod is Running and `kubectl get endpoints` lists the Service endpoint. What should you check next?
choices: The Service's clusterIP allocation inside the cluster CIDR — a colliding ClusterIP would prevent external reachability on the NodePort
The pod's readinessProbe configuration and timing, since a flapping readiness check intermittently drops the NodePort backend
Whether kube-proxy is in IPVS rather than iptables mode, since IPVS rejects NodePort traffic from off-cluster sources by default
Whether the host firewall or cloud security group permits inbound traffic to the node on TCP 30080 in the NodePort range
questions.explanation: Pod Running + endpoint listed means kube-proxy has already programmed the iptables/IPVS rule, so anything reaching the node on 30080 would be forwarded. The remaining hop is the network in front of the node. The most common blocker is the host firewall (iptables, ufw, firewalld) or the cloud security group failing to allow the NodePort range (30000-32767). The clusterIP is irrelevant to external traffic. A failing readinessProbe would have removed the pod from endpoints. IPVS vs iptables mode changes packet handling but never blocks all traffic on its own.

questions.q: You need to expose a Service externally using a cloud provider's load balancer. Which Service type should you use?
choices: ExternalName
NodePort
ClusterIP with externalIPs set to the load balancer IP
LoadBalancer
questions.explanation: Service type LoadBalancer asks the cloud-controller-manager to provision a real external load balancer (AWS NLB/ALB, GCP TCP/HTTP(S) LB, Azure Standard LB) and assign it an externally reachable IP or hostname. NodePort only opens a port on every node — fronting it with a load balancer is left to the operator. ExternalName is a DNS CNAME alias to an out-of-cluster name; it doesn't expose anything. ClusterIP + externalIPs is for advertising an existing external IP onto the cluster, not for asking a cloud provider to provision one.

questions.q: You need a Service that maps `legacy.internal` inside the cluster to an external hostname `legacy.example.com` without proxying traffic. Which Service type achieves this?
choices: ExternalName with spec.externalName: legacy.example.com
ClusterIP with an Endpoints object pointing to the external IP
LoadBalancer with an annotation pointing to legacy.example.com
Headless Service with a manual DNS CNAME record
questions.explanation: ExternalName tells CoreDNS to answer queries for the Service name with a CNAME to `spec.externalName`. No clusterIP is allocated, no kube-proxy rule is installed, and the calling pod resolves the alias and connects directly. A ClusterIP + Endpoints object would require the external service to be reachable by IP and would proxy through kube-proxy. LoadBalancer provisions an inbound load balancer, not a DNS alias. Headless Services return pod IPs from a selector, not external CNAMEs.

nodes.title: Trace a pod-creation request

data.scenario: You run `kubectl apply -f pod.yaml`. Order the Kubernetes components the request flows through.

nodes.explanation: kubectl sends the spec to the kube-apiserver, which persists desired state to etcd; the kube-scheduler assigns a node; the kubelet on that node instructs the container runtime to start the pod.

nodes.title: Mixed exam topics: Key Ideas
nodes.content: Some exam objectives don't fit neatly into a single domain — they span protocols, tools, or concepts covered briefly in multiple sections. These cards treat each item as a stand-alone fact, the way an exam question presents it: one concept, one answer.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between a hub, a switch, and a router?
flashcards.back: Hub: Layer 1, repeats every frame to all ports — all devices share bandwidth, collisions guaranteed. Switch: Layer 2, forwards frames using a MAC address table to only the destination port — full duplex, no collisions, each port gets full bandwidth. Router: Layer 3, makes forwarding decisions based on IP address, connects different networks. Hub is legacy; switches dominate LAN; routers are at network edges.

flashcards.front: What is RAID 5 and how many drives can it tolerate losing?
flashcards.back: RAID 5 stripes data and parity across at least 3 drives. Any single drive failure can be recovered by reconstructing missing data from the remaining drives and parity. It cannot tolerate 2 simultaneous drive failures. Effective capacity = (N-1) × drive size. Read performance is excellent; write requires parity recalculation. RAID 6 tolerates 2 failures using double parity.

flashcards.front: What does a proxy server do, and how does a forward proxy differ from a reverse proxy?
flashcards.back: Forward proxy: sits between clients and the internet on behalf of clients — used for content filtering, caching, and anonymizing outbound requests (the server sees the proxy's IP). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers on behalf of the server — used for load balancing, SSL termination, caching, and hiding backend topology (the client sees the proxy's IP). Both intermediate HTTP, but they protect opposite sides.

flashcards.front: What is the purpose of a DMZ in network architecture?
flashcards.back: A demilitarized zone is a network segment between the untrusted internet and the trusted internal network, typically protected by two firewalls (or two interfaces on one firewall). Public-facing services (web, email, DNS) sit in the DMZ: internet can reach them but not the internal network; if the DMZ host is compromised, the inner firewall still blocks access to the internal LAN.

questions.q: You need to take a snapshot backup of etcd running as a static pod. The data directory is /var/lib/etcd and certificates live in /etc/kubernetes/pki/etcd/. Which command correctly creates a snapshot the cluster can later restore from?
choices: etcdctl backup --data-dir /var/lib/etcd --backup-dir /backup/etcd.db --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --tls --auto-compaction
etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd.db --data-dir /var/lib/etcd --skip-tls-verify --endpoints=127.0.0.1:2379 --watch-progress
ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd.db --endpoints=https://127.0.0.1:2379 --cacert=.../etcd/ca.crt --cert=.../server.crt --key=.../server.key
kubectl -n kube-system exec etcd-master -- etcdctl snapshot save /backup/etcd.db --tls --insecure-skip-tls-verify
questions.explanation: `etcdctl snapshot save` is the v3 API command and must talk to the live cluster over TLS, so it needs --endpoints, --cacert, --cert and --key. `etcdctl backup` is the deprecated v2 syntax that operated on the offline data directory. Passing --data-dir to `snapshot save` is invalid — that flag belongs to the etcd server, not the snapshot client. Running it through `kubectl exec` without mounting the host PKI still fails because the etcd container can't read the host certs without --cacert/--cert/--key.

questions.q: After restoring an etcd snapshot to a new data directory /var/lib/etcd-restore, what must change so the etcd static pod starts using the restored data?
choices: Run `kubeadm etcd restore /var/lib/etcd-restore` so kubeadm registers the new directory and recreates the etcd static-pod manifest
Edit /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml so both the --data-dir flag and the backing hostPath volume point at /var/lib/etcd-restore
Delete the etcd pod with `kubectl delete pod etcd-master -n kube-system` so the kubelet rebuilds it with the restored directory
Run `systemctl restart etcd` on the control-plane node after creating a symlink from /var/lib/etcd to the restored directory
questions.explanation: etcd runs as a static pod managed by the kubelet. Both the --data-dir flag passed to the etcd container AND the hostPath volume that backs that directory must be updated in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd.yaml; the kubelet sees the manifest change and recreates the pod against the restored data. `kubeadm etcd restore` does not exist. Deleting the pod alone is useless because the kubelet recreates it from the unchanged manifest, still pointing at the old directory. There is no etcd systemd service on a kubeadm-managed control plane — etcd runs only as a static pod.

questions.q: A static pod manifest placed in /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ is not starting. The pod does not appear in `kubectl get pods -A`. What should you check first?
choices: Confirm the pod is listed in `kubectl get pods --field-selector=status.phase=Pending`
Verify the pod has a valid ServiceAccount token mounted
Check the kube-scheduler logs for scheduling errors
Check the kubelet logs on the node where the manifest was placed (`journalctl -u kubelet`)
questions.explanation: Static pods are owned end-to-end by the kubelet on the node where their manifest lives — the API server only ever sees the mirror pod once kubelet creates it. If the mirror pod never appears, the kubelet is the only component that knows why (YAML parse error, image pull failure, file permission). `journalctl -u kubelet` is where those errors land. The scheduler is uninvolved (static pods are pre-bound to the local node). Filtering Pending pods won't find one that was never registered, and a missing token wouldn't keep the pod manifest from being created in the first place.

questions.q: The kube-scheduler pod is not running after a cluster upgrade. It is defined as a static pod. Where would you find its manifest to investigate?
choices: /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler.yaml
/var/lib/kubelet/config/kube-scheduler.yaml
/opt/kubernetes/scheduler/kube-scheduler.yaml
/etc/systemd/system/kube-scheduler.service
questions.explanation: In a kubeadm-provisioned cluster the kubelet watches /etc/kubernetes/manifests/ for static-pod manifests for kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager, kube-scheduler and etcd. A bad flag, wrong image tag or YAML typo there would prevent kube-scheduler from starting. /var/lib/kubelet/config holds the kubelet's own ComponentConfig. There is no /opt/kubernetes/scheduler path in a kubeadm install. kube-scheduler runs as a static pod, not a systemd unit.

questions.q: A Deployment named 'web-app' has 5 replicas but only 3 pods are running. `kubectl describe deployment web-app` shows the ReplicaSet has 5 desired but 3 available. What is the most appropriate next diagnostic step?
choices: Scale the Deployment down to 3 replicas to match the current state
Delete and recreate the Deployment with the same spec
Run `kubectl get pods -l app=web-app`, then `kubectl describe pod <pod-name>` on any non-running pod
Run `kubectl rollout restart deployment/web-app` immediately
questions.explanation: When desired > available, the individual pods carry the diagnostic information. Listing pods by the Deployment selector reveals which two are stuck (Pending, ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff), and `kubectl describe pod` surfaces the Events explaining why — image pull failure, insufficient resources, missing PVC, failing readiness, etc. Scaling down hides the symptom without explaining it. Deleting and recreating throws away the same diagnostic state. A rollout restart kicks pods that may already be unable to schedule, which doesn't address the root cause.

questions.q: A Deployment rolling update is stuck. `kubectl rollout status deployment/api` hangs with `1 old replicas are pending termination`. Which command best helps you find which pod is blocking the rollout?
choices: `kubectl delete replicaset <old-rs-name>` and let the Deployment recover
`kubectl get replicasets -l app=api` to compare desired and ready counts
`kubectl rollout pause deployment/api` to freeze the in-flight rollout
`kubectl describe pod <old-pod>` to inspect termination events, preStop hooks and graceful-shutdown timing
questions.explanation: Pods that won't terminate usually have one of three issues, all visible from `describe pod`: a long preStop hook, a process ignoring SIGTERM, or a high `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`. Listing replicasets shows counts but not the why. Deleting the old ReplicaSet bypasses the diagnostic and risks orphaning pods. Pausing the rollout freezes it without explaining why the old pod is hanging.

questions.q: A NetworkPolicy is applied to pods labeled `app=api`. After applying it, the API pods can no longer reach the database pods labeled `app=db` on port 5432. The policy spec includes `policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]` and an empty `egress: []`. Why?
choices: NetworkPolicies only apply to ingress traffic, so egress should still work
Empty `egress: []` combined with `policyTypes: Egress` is interpreted as 'deny all egress' for the selected pods
The policy must be in the same namespace as the database pods to allow traffic
NetworkPolicies do not apply to TCP traffic on port 5432 without explicit protocol specification
questions.explanation: Once `policyTypes` includes Egress, the egress section becomes a closed allow-list: an empty list means 'no rule matches, deny all egress' for the selected pods. You must add an egress rule that lets traffic to the db pods on port 5432 (typically using a podSelector). The first option is wrong — egress is included whenever `policyTypes` says so. NetworkPolicies are namespace-scoped, but cross-namespace egress is expressed by `namespaceSelector`, not by colocating the policy. Protocol defaults to TCP, so the last option is also wrong.

questions.q: After applying a new NetworkPolicy, pods in namespace `app` can no longer reach the kube-dns Service (10.96.0.10:53). What must be added so DNS works again?
choices: A podSelector that matches the kube-dns pods inside the same policy object, with no further namespace targeting
An egress rule on the policy allowing UDP and TCP port 53 to the kube-system namespace (or directly to the kube-dns pods)
A namespaceSelector allowing all ingress from kube-system to the app pods, so kube-dns can reply through that channel
An ingress rule allowing the kube-dns Service to reach the app pods on port 53 in both UDP and TCP directions
questions.explanation: Once a NetworkPolicy with `policyTypes: Egress` selects a pod, every outbound destination is denied unless an egress rule permits it. DNS resolution requires the app pods to reach CoreDNS in kube-system on UDP/TCP 53, so the rule needs `to: [namespaceSelector kube-system]` (or a podSelector for kube-dns) plus `ports: [{port: 53, protocol: UDP/TCP}]`. A podSelector alone, without a namespaceSelector, only matches pods in the policy's own namespace. Ingress rules govern inbound traffic and never restore outbound resolution.
